title: Margaret River takes home most trophies of any region worldwide at 2026 IWSC
summary:
Margaret River Wine Region has been awarded the most trophies of any region in the world at the 2026 International Wine and Spirit Competition (IWSC). Judged from more than 6,000 global entries by leading wine critics, buyers and sommeliers, Margaret River wines were awarded six trophies, contributing to Australia’s total haul of eight, and positioning the country alongside France as the competition’s leading wine nation. Following the initial judging in Margaret River in August, the region’s gold medal-winning wines progressed to the next stage of the competition, where they were judged alongside gold medal wines from around the world. From this international field, the trophy winners were selected as the best wines in their respective categories. “We’re at the beginning of a new chapter for Australian wine in the UK,” said IWSC judge Freddy Bulmer, wine buyer of The Wine Society in the UK. “We are definitely seeing Margaret River really overperforming against the rest of the country.”

content:
The Margaret River region scored six trophies. Image supplied

Margaret River Wine Region has been awarded the most trophies of any region in the world at the 2026 International Wine and Spirit Competition (IWSC).

Judged from more than 6,000 global entries by leading wine critics, buyers and sommeliers, Margaret River wines were awarded six trophies, contributing to Australia’s total haul of eight, and positioning the country alongside France as the competition’s leading wine nation.

Following the initial judging in Margaret River in August, the region’s gold medal-winning wines progressed to the next stage of the competition, where they were judged alongside gold medal wines from around the world. From this international field, the trophy winners were selected as the best wines in their respective categories.

“We’re at the beginning of a new chapter for Australian wine in the UK,” said IWSC judge Freddy Bulmer, wine buyer of The Wine Society in the UK.

“We are definitely seeing Margaret River really overperforming against the rest of the country.”

Three of Margaret River’s trophies were awarded to Cabernet Sauvignon: Lenton Brae Cabernet Sauvignon 2024, Nocturne Single Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon 2024 and Stella Bella Wines Suckfizzle Cabernet Sauvignon 2024.

Stella Bella said the award is also further recognition of the distinctive character of Cabernet grown in the southern reaches of Margaret River. Suckfizzle is the winery’s most southerly vineyard, “an exposed maritime site where cooler growing conditions, ocean influence and a long ripening season are central to the wine’s character”.

“To win gold was already a fantastic result, but to then have the wine put back in front of the judges alongside more than 250 gold medal wines and emerge with one of just 45 trophies makes this incredibly special,” said Jarrod Olsen, chief winemaker at Stella Bella.

“Suckfizzle has always been a wine defined by where it comes from. It’s our most southern site, wild, unbridled and heavily influenced by the Indian and Southern Oceans. It’s the place of origin that gives this Cabernet its unique energy, structure and personality and we work tirelessly in the vineyard and winery to capture, harness and emphasise that each vintage.

“We’re incredibly proud of the wine, but we’re also proud to see Margaret River perform so strongly. Six trophies from one region on an international stage says a lot about the quality of wine being grown here.”

Chardonnay also made its mark, with trophies awarded to Xanadu Wines Reserve Chardonnay 2024 and the record-scoring House of Cards Ace High Chardonnay 2025, which achieved 100 points. A further trophy went to Willespie Estate Wilyabrup Reserve Semillon 2025.

CEO of Margaret River Wine Association Penny Dickeson said these global trophies reinforce the quality and consistency of wine across every level of producer in the region.

“Margaret River wineries have made the most of a remarkable run of consistent growing seasons to produce wines of exceptional quality. Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay continue to be judged among the finest examples of their kind in Australia and internationally, and these IWSC results are a wonderful recognition of the dedication and talent of our region’s family-owned wineries,” Dickeson said.

A total of 45 wine trophies were awarded across ‘still’, ‘sparkling’, and ‘sweet & fortified’ categories by the IWSC judging committee. The IWSC trophy-winning wines will be eligible for section in the IWSC 2026 Producer Trophy winners, which will be revealed in November.

title: SAWIA appoints executive committee for 2026/2027
summary:
The South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA) has appointed its executive committee for 2026/2027, with Kirsty Balnaves continuing as president and Tom Keelan re-elected as vice president. SAWIA said the 13-member executive committee brings together growers, winemakers and business leaders from across South Australia’s wine regions and supply chain, “providing industry-led direction as the sector continues to navigate significant change and pursue new opportunities”. The executive committee was announced at SAWIA’s annual general meeting on 6 October 2026, “which reflected on the association’s activities, achievements and advocacy during 2025/26”.

The post SAWIA appoints executive committee for 2026/2027 appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Tom Keelan and Kirsty Balnaves. Image supplied

The South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA) has appointed its executive committee for 2026/2027, with Kirsty Balnaves continuing as president and Tom Keelan re-elected as vice president.

SAWIA said the 13-member executive committee brings together growers, winemakers and business leaders from across South Australia’s wine regions and supply chain, “providing industry-led direction as the sector continues to navigate significant change and pursue new opportunities”.

The executive committee was announced at SAWIA’s annual general meeting on 6 October 2026, “which reflected on the association’s activities, achievements and advocacy during 2025/26”.

The executive committee is comprised from the SAWIA membership and consists of seven area representatives nominated by South Australia’s main wine regional associations, and six representatives from SAWIA’s broader membership.

Members of the SAWIA Executive Committee for 2026/27 are:

  • Kirsty Balnaves, Balnaves of Coonawarra, Coonawarra Grape & Wine (president)
  • Tom Keelan, The Pawn Wine Co, Langhorne Creek Grape & Wine (vice president)
  • Paul Zerella, Project Wine
  • Anthony Catanzariti, Treasury Wine Estates
  • Danielle Arnfield, Vinarchy
  • Louisa Rose, Hill-Smith Family Estates
  • Jeremy Blanks, Tarac
  • Lucy Clements, Freestone Estate
  • Olivia Hoffmann-Barry, Jim Barry Wines, Clare Valley Wine & Grape Association
  • Ben Riggs, Mr Riggs Wine Co, McLaren Vale Grape, Wine & Tourism Association
  • Brigid Nolan, The Wine Group, Riverland Wine Industry Development Council
  • Alex Trescowthick, Trescowthick Wines, Adelaide Hills Wine Region
  • Matthew McCulloch, Langmeil Winery, Barossa Grape & Wine Association

SAWIA president Kirsty Balnaves thanked the members of the SAWIA executive committee who volunteer their time and lead SAWIA with accountability and foresight, delivering value to members.

“The strength of the executive committee is its direct connection to the industry it represents. These people are living and breathing South Australian grapes and wine. They understand firsthand the decisions growers and wine businesses are making because they are facing the same challenges and opportunities in their own businesses,” Balnaves said.

“That industry knowledge helps shape what SAWIA advocates for, where we invest our resources and the programs and services we deliver for members and the South Australian wine industry.

“The future of our industry will not look exactly like the past. We need to continue to evolve as markets change, lead in finding new opportunities and unite around what we can achieve together.”

title: Murray Street Vineyards sold to family-owned A.G. Oatley Wines
summary:
Sandy Oatley and his daughter Nicky Oatley of A.G. Oatley Wines have purchased award-winning Barossa Valley winery Murray Street Vineyards at Greenock Estate. The purchase includes the modern winery, the cellar door and vineyard holdings. "Murray Street Vineyards has built an outstanding reputation in the Barossa, and we're honoured to be its next custodians," said Sandy Oatley. Founded in 2001 by William (Bill) Jahnke and Andrew Seppelt, Murray Street Vineyards became fully family-owned in 2014 when Janai Brengman joined her father as co-owner. title: TWE cuts 170 jobs as new operating model comes into effect
summary:
According to reporting by The Australian, Treasury Wine Estates (TWE) has axed 170 roles as part of its previously announced major operational and regional restructure. The article details that the redundancies are mostly across roles in marketing, IT, finance and support roles at TWE’s offices. The Australian said that some job losses are believed to have hit its vineyards, however, majority of the redundancies are at the winery’s Melbourne headquarters and other offices. “We recognise the impact of these changes on our people and thank those leaving us for their contribution,” a TWE spokesperson told The Australian.

The post TWE cuts 170 jobs as new operating model comes into effect appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Sam Fischer, CEO of TWE. Image courtesy TWE

According to reporting by The Australian, Treasury Wine Estates (TWE) has axed 170 roles as part of its previously announced major operational and regional restructure.

The article details that the redundancies are mostly across roles in marketing, IT, finance and support roles at TWE’s offices.

The Australian said that some job losses are believed to have hit its vineyards, however, majority of the redundancies are at the winery’s Melbourne headquarters and other offices.

“We recognise the impact of these changes on our people and thank those leaving us for their contribution,” a TWE spokesperson told The Australian.

“At the same time, we’re continuing to invest for growth, including recruiting for new roles primarily across our commercial teams in Australia and New Zealand, as well as China and emerging markets, focused on our portfolio of priority brands including Penfolds, DAOU and Matua.”

The wine company revealed back in April that it planned to focus on creating a unified, simplified portfolio and that the new operating model for the company would be effective as of 1 October 2026.

TWE returned ownership of the Rouge Homme brand to the Redman family in May and more recently announced the sale of Seppelt to Aaron Drummond, CEO and co-owner of Stonier.

title: Alkina Wine Estate purchases Eden Valley vineyard ‘Trial Hill’
summary:
Alkina Wine Estate has purchased the historic Trial Hill vineyard in Eden Valley, South Australia, from Barossa vigneron Joel Mattschoss. The isolated, elevated property spans 24 hectares, with approximately eight hectares currently planted to Grenache, Shiraz, Riesling and Chardonnay. Alkina said it will join its original 43-hectare vineyard at Greenock, “expanding the estate’s holdings within the Barossa and providing an important Eden Valley counterpoint through old vines grown at altitude”. Situated near Pewsey Vale in Eden Valley, the Trial Hill vineyard was historically part of the original Pewsey Vale property established by Joseph Gilbert, who planted the area’s first vines in 1847. “We have a long-held belief that the great wines of the world come from truly great sites,” said Alkina owner Alejandro Bulgheroni. “Markets and styles may change, but places with real individuality, history and the capacity to create distinctive wines will endure. This belief underpins our confidence that Australian Grenache can sit comfortably amongst the great wines of the world, and we believe this historic site in Eden Valley will further enable us to explore that potential.”

The post Alkina Wine Estate purchases Eden Valley vineyard ‘Trial Hill’ appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The Trial Hill vineyard, which has been purchased by Alkina Wine Estate. Image supplied

Alkina Wine Estate has purchased the historic Trial Hill vineyard in Eden Valley, South Australia, from Barossa vigneron Joel Mattschoss.

The isolated, elevated property spans 24 hectares, with approximately eight hectares currently planted to Grenache, Shiraz, Riesling and Chardonnay. Alkina said it will join its original 43-hectare vineyard at Greenock, “expanding the estate’s holdings within the Barossa and providing an important Eden Valley counterpoint through old vines grown at altitude”.

Situated near Pewsey Vale in Eden Valley, the Trial Hill vineyard was historically part of the original Pewsey Vale property established by Joseph Gilbert, who planted the area’s first vines in 1847.

“We have a long-held belief that the great wines of the world come from truly great sites,” said Alkina owner Alejandro Bulgheroni.

“Markets and styles may change, but places with real individuality, history and the capacity to create distinctive wines will endure. This belief underpins our confidence that Australian Grenache can sit comfortably amongst the great wines of the world, and we believe this historic site in Eden Valley will further enable us to explore that potential.”

Today, the vineyard’s contour-planted Grenache, Shiraz and Riesling vines are approximately 80 years old and sit between 450 and 480 metres above sea level, overlooking the Barossa Valley below.

“I have admired this beautiful vineyard for many years, with its sweeping views across the Barossa and extraordinary amphitheatre-like contours,” added Amelia Nolan, Alkina winemaker and managing director.

“Old Grenache vines at this altitude are a finite resource in Australia and deserve to be preserved and nurtured. Our terroir work at Greenock has shown us just how much geological complexity can exist within a relatively small area, and Trial Hill gives us the opportunity to continue that exploration in a completely different landscape.

“We are very grateful to Joel Mattschoss for considering Alkina to be a fitting future custodian of such a special place.”

Mattschoss said that Trial Hill is a vineyard he had imagined himself holding onto for the long term, and so, the decision to part with it was not one he took lightly.

“Having followed Alkina’s work at Greenock, I felt there was a natural fit, and I’m very pleased to be handing over custodianship to a team that will respect what is already there while taking the vineyard’s potential to another level.”

The property rises steeply to approximately 550 metres at its highest point. Alkina explained its medium-term plans include establishing an additional terraced, bush-vine Grenache vineyard on these upper slopes, which would place it among the highest Grenache vineyards in Australia.

At Trial Hill, Alkina will extend the micro-terroir work first undertaken at its Greenock estate with terroir specialist Pedro Parra in 2017. Detailed mapping of the site’s geology will commence in 2027, with the intention of “identifying and defining individual terroirs that may ultimately sit within Alkina’s renowned range of ‘Polygon’ wines”.

The winery noted that initial exploratory work “suggests a complex geological landscape, where deeply weathered quartzite and schist have broken down over time to form sandy, freedraining soils”. This creates a “distinctly different terroir” from its Greenock vineyard, which is “characterised by schist, limestone and ferrous clay”.

title: Three winemakers, one parcel of grapes: Inside MyattsField’s interactive project
summary:
As wineries increasingly look for innovative ways to bring consumers to the cellar door, MyattsField Vineyards in Western Australia’s Bickley Valley has been running an experience they call the ‘Tête-à-Tête à Trois (TTT) project’. Translating to ‘Head to Head by Three’, the project began in 2015 as a “light-hearted internal challenge” between three winemakers. The premise is that a single parcel of fruit is harvested at the exact same time and divided equally among three winemakers — Rachael Davenport, Josh Davenport and Josh Uren. Working independently, each winemaker applies their own philosophy, techniques, vessels and oak selections to create three wildly different, small-batch expressions from the same underlying fruit. "The idea was born out of pure curiosity and a desire to pull back the curtain on how different winemaking choices shape a wine," said founder Josh Davenport.

The post Three winemakers, one parcel of grapes: Inside MyattsField’s interactive project appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The three wines together: The Flyer (Rachael Davenport), The Founder (Josh Davenport) and The Factotum (Josh Uren). Images supplied

As wineries increasingly look for innovative ways to bring consumers to the cellar door, MyattsField Vineyards in Western Australia’s Bickley Valley has been running an experience they call the ‘Tête-à-Tête à Trois (TTT) project’.

Translating to ‘Head to Head by Three’, the project began in 2015 as a “light-hearted internal challenge” between three winemakers.

The premise is that a single parcel of fruit is harvested at the exact same time and divided equally among three winemakers — Rachael Davenport, Josh Davenport and Josh Uren. Working independently, each winemaker applies their own philosophy, techniques, vessels and oak selections to create three wildly different, small-batch expressions from the same underlying fruit.

“The idea was born out of pure curiosity and a desire to pull back the curtain on how different winemaking choices shape a wine,” said founder Josh Davenport.

“We often sit at the blending bench and see how dramatically a single variable can change the final profile. Rather than keeping that process behind cellar doors, we turned it into an interactive experience that invites wine lovers right into the winemaking room with us.”

Josh and Rachael Davenport.

Over the years, TTT has featured Chardonnay, Shiraz, Rosé, Pinot Noir and Zinfandel. For 2026, the team focused on Chenin Blanc, which was “hand-harvested from a very warm 2024 vintage grown on ironstone gravels and clay soils”. Chosen for its high natural acidity and structural versatility, the winery said Chenin Blanc is the ideal varietal to demonstrate how winemaking techniques can impact style.

The TTT project nowadays serves as a bridge between production and tasting, with the winery calling it an “innovative engagement model” for the cellar door.

The final vote for the best wine will be handed over to the audience across two tasting sessions inside the winery on 17 and 18 October. The public is invited to come meet the winemakers and join sessions of “personal preference and side-by-side discovery” that aim to dismantle traditional wine pretension.

“For us, it’s a brilliant playground to experiment with micro-batches,” said Davenport.

“Consumers have an incredibly sharp, intuitive palate when given the chance to compare side by side. Seeing how people react keeps our instincts fresh and reminds us there is never just one ‘right’ way to make a great wine.”

He added that the experience transforms wine tasting into an “active discovery”.

“It gives people a rare, hands-on look at the variables that define flavour, stripping away pretension and giving them the confidence to talk about what they’re tasting.”

The winery said this open-door philosophy highlights its own forward-thinking strategy and the creative vitality of the Perth Hills region.

MyattsField Vineyards in the Perth Hills.

“It sits right at the heart of what we do.

“We aren’t afraid to push boundaries. Boutique winemaking here is as much about innovation and creative freedom as it is about tradition. At the end of the day, wine is meant to provoke conversation. Tête-à-Tête à Trois gets people talking, debating, and discovering what they truly enjoy in a glass.”

Customers are even able to purchase 3-packs of the challenge wines and conduct their own blind tasting showdowns at home.

The post NSW Container Deposit Scheme update sees improved terms for small and medium wineries appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
It has been announced that glass wine bottles will be included in the NSW Container Deposit Scheme, ‘Return and Earn’, when it expands from July 2027.

NSW Wine said this change will have a fair-reaching impact on every wine business that sells into NSW.

“Since the expansion was announced, NSW Wine has worked closely with government and the scheme coordinator, advocating consistently for measures that reduce cost and administrative burden for our members and give the wine industry a voice at the table,” it said.

Last Thursday, the scheme coordinator Exchange for Change (EfC) announced a package of changes, “made in direct response to NSW wine industry input and advocacy, that will ease the impact of the scheme on small and medium wine producers”.

EfC will hold NSW supplier contribution pricing at current rates for a further 12 months, up to and including the January 2028 invoice. For wine producers, this means the glass rate remains at 14.03 cents per container.

From July 2027, EfC will also:

  • Introduce a new Micro Supplier Program for businesses supplying up to 100,000 containers per year, with annual reporting and annual invoicing.
  • Increase the Small Supplier Program threshold from 300,000 to 1 million containers per year, with quarterly reporting and quarterly invoicing.
  • Extend payment terms for micro and small suppliers from 7 to 28 days.

Suppliers who prefer to remain on monthly reporting and invoicing will be able to opt out.

“We’re pleased to announce these changes today in direct response to feedback from the beverage industry,” said Danielle Smalley, CEO of Exchange for Change.

“Approximately 86 per cent of currently participating beverage suppliers will, from 1 July next year, benefit from these changes which mean less administration and less effort to participate in the NSW scheme, in addition to the suppliers who will be joining the scheme when it expands from mid-2027.

“We would like to thank industry for your feedback and ongoing participation in the NSW container deposit scheme.”

NSW Wine president Mark Bourne said the changes are practical, sensible and will make a real difference for its members.

“Reduced reporting requirements and higher thresholds will significantly lower the administrative burden for NSW wine businesses, and 28-day payment terms reflect normal business practice.”

NSW Wine flagged that wine businesses that sell into ACT should note arrangements there differ. EfC will introduce Micro (up to 100,000 containers) and Small (up to 300,000 containers) Supplier Programs in the ACT from July 2027, but payment terms will remain 7 days, and new ACT pricing applies from the February 2027 invoice, with glass moving from 16.27 to 16.24 cents per container.

NSW Wine said it will continue to advocate on behalf of the wine industry to further reduce the impact on producers in any way it can as July 2027 approaches.

title: Coal River Valley winery wins national trophy at the 2026 Australian Pinot Noir Challenge
summary:
Young Coal River Valley winery Decades has been named the 2026 Australian Pinot Noir Challenge national trophy winner with its 2025 Pinot Noir, emerging from 319 entries across 20 regions. The challenge brings Pinot Noir from across the country into a single national field. In order to win the trophy, a wine must first stand out among its regional peers, then prevail against the other regional winners. This year’s final field spanned Tasmania, six Victorian regions and Western Australia. “With 319 entries from 20 regions across Australia, this year’s Challenge showcased the exceptional quality of the 2025 vintage and the strength of Australian Pinot Noir,” said Tom Carson, chair of judges.

The post Coal River Valley winery wins national trophy at the 2026 Australian Pinot Noir Challenge appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Decades has won the national trophy at the challenge just four years after purchasing the vineyard. Image courtesy Australian Pinot Noir Challenge via Instagram

Young Coal River Valley winery Decades has been named the 2026 Australian Pinot Noir Challenge national trophy winner with its 2025 Pinot Noir, emerging from 319 entries across 20 regions.

The challenge brings Pinot Noir from across the country into a single national field. In order to win the trophy, a wine must first stand out among its regional peers, then prevail against the other regional winners. This year’s final field spanned Tasmania, six Victorian regions and Western Australia.

“With 319 entries from 20 regions across Australia, this year’s Challenge showcased the exceptional quality of the 2025 vintage and the strength of Australian Pinot Noir,” said Tom Carson, chair of judges.

“Against that outstanding field, the 2025 Decades Pinot Noir from Tasmania’s Coal River Valley absolutely captivated the judges from its first showing. Its wonderful aromatics, detail and silky palate carried it through every stage of judging. To win the national trophy with only their third release is an extraordinary achievement for Steve Flamsteed and Brad Rogers.”

For Steve Flamsteed and Brad Rogers, the result gives their Coal River Valley project a national stage just four years after they purchased the vineyard. Friends since their days at Roseworthy College, the pair built Decades around a shared ambition to make wine together.

“It’s an incredible honour to have been selected as the winner by that exceptional group of judges out of what would have been a stack of beautiful wines. Australian Pinot (and Chardonnay) is in such an incredible place right now and wine shows and events like the Pinot Challenge just push us to keep getting better,” said Steve Flamsteed, owner of Decades Wine.

The winning Pinot Noir impressed the judges with its “vibrant cherry fruit and spice, fresh blood orange acidity, fine tannins and a long, beautifully balanced finish”.

The trophy returns to Tasmania after the Yarra Valley’s Giant Steps broke a five-year Tasmanian winning streak in 2025. Tasmania was strongly represented throughout this year’s judging, producing “more than 45 per cent of all gold-medal wines”.

The national win follows Decades being named ‘2027 Best New Winery’ and Flamsteed recognised as ‘2027 Winemaker of the Year’ by Halliday Wine Companion.

Victoria claimed six of the eight regional trophies, “demonstrating the variety’s success across different growing areas”. The results also brought first regional trophies for Great Western, won by Best’s Wines, and Sunbury, won by Marnong Estate.

The 2026 regional winners are:

  • Tasmania: Decades — 2025 Decades Pinot Noir
  • Mornington Peninsula: Merli — 2025 Merli Pinot Noir
  • Yarra Valley: Oakridge Wines — 2025 Vineyard Series Hazeldene Pinot Noir
  • Gippsland: Dirty Three Wines — 2025 “Dirt 2” Pinot Noir
  • Sunbury: Marnong Estate — 2025 Weatherstone Single Vineyard Pinot Noir
  • Great Western: Best’s Wines — 2025 Best’s Great Western Pinot Noir
  • Macedon Ranges: Curly Flat Vineyard — 2024 Curly Flat Estate Pinot Noir
  • Mount Barker, WA: Howard Park Wines — 2025 Marchand & Burch Village Pinot Noir

title: How a Mornington Peninsula vineyard used contact bioherbicide to get on top of glyphosate resistant ryegrass
summary:

Managing weeds is a constant and ongoing challenge in a vineyard setting, and it’s crucial to making every other process run more smoothly. Not only do they interfere with the quality and yield of grapes, but they can wreak havoc on irrigation systems, create shelter for pests, and increase labour costs.

The post How a Mornington Peninsula vineyard used contact bioherbicide to get on top of glyphosate resistant ryegrass appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
After years of losing ground to glyphosate resistant ryegrass, a Victorian vineyard found its answer through changing the mode of action.

Managing weeds is a constant and ongoing challenge in a vineyard setting, and it’s crucial to making every other process run more smoothly. Not only do they interfere with the quality and yield of grapes, but they can wreak havoc on irrigation systems, create shelter for pests, and increase labour costs.

For one Victorian vineyard, annual ryegrass with a resistance to glyphosate had become so prolific an issue that it could be seen from satellite imagery.

“The absence of a solution wasn’t from lack of trying,” says Richard Hall, Head of Agricultural Sales and Agronomy at Contact BioSolutions. “The vineyard had worked through different tank mixes and application machinery, with limited results. What kept the ryegrass in check, to the extent anything did, was manual labour.” A process which is slow, costly, and never finished.

“It’s not the favourite job on the vineyard to do,” explains Richard, “but it’s important to get on top of it before it continues to spread.”

Limited pathways for addressing vineyard weeds

Most Australian vineyards, organic or conventional, already manage weeds with a combination of tools. Mid-row cover crops add nitrogen to the soil, while summer irrigation and cultivation reduce weeds before they can establish. Under the vine, mechanical control and herbicides, both synthetic and biological, fill the gaps.

Once resistance has taken hold however, more of the same chemistry won’t fix it, and the alternatives narrow quickly. Cultivation under the vine risks damaging roots, irrigation and trunks, and hand weeding across a commercial block is rarely viable for long.

“Adding a range of options to your weed management toolkit is always worthwhile, and perhaps never more so than now,” says Richard. “Every situation is different: it’s about managing weeds rather than aiming to fully eradicate, so that we maintain the presence of things like native grasses and clover in vineyards for example, to suit the grower’s unique requirements.”

Chemical options are about to narrow further, following the final APVMA review of traditional contact herbicides paraquat and diquat. This has left growers who rely on these fast-acting knockdowns under the vine with two years to find an alternative.

Changing the mode of action

What the Mornington Peninsula vineyard needed was a different way of killing the weed. The solution was found through a tank mix of FireHawk® Bioherbicide Super Concentrate and glufosinate.

FireHawk works in a fundamentally different way to glyphosate. Glyphosate is absorbed by the plant and moved through it to act systematically. FireHawk acts on contact, breaking through the plant’s protective barriers and rapidly desiccating green tissue, targeting broadleaf weeds and grasses.

“For a contact bioherbicide, thorough coverage is key: spray unwanted plants until the foliage is wet to the point of run-off,” explains Richard. “For best results, apply in full sun and target weeds while they’re small and actively growing. At medium weed density, the recommended spray application rate is 750 L/ha. Where weed pressure is high, or when spot spraying, increase this to 1000 L/ha.”

For the Mornington Peninsula vineyard, FireHawk’s mode of action was key. Because FireHawk doesn’t rely on a systemic pathway, the ryegrass’s resistance to glyphosate offered it no protection.

“The effect was visible within hours, with treated areas browning off while untreated ground stayed green,” shares Richard. “After years of the problem getting worse, the grower is now getting on top of it.”

What’s in the drum

FireHawk Bioherbicide Super Concentrate is a 777 g/L formulation of nonanoic acid, carrying the highest active loading of any product of its kind on the market. Nonanoic acid occurs naturally in a range of plants, including geraniums.

It is non-selective and controls a range of common annual and perennial broadleaf weeds and grasses. The label allows rates from 2 to 5 L per 100 L, so growers can match the rate to what’s in front of them: lower rates for young, actively growing weeds and routine maintenance, and higher rates once weeds have matured.

For vineyards, a few practical points stand out. “We have no withholding periods,” Dr Frank Glatz, Founder and Managing Director of Contact BioSolutions says. “We’re exempt from maximum residue food limits because our product is already in food chains.”

FireHawk leaves no residual herbicide activity in the soil and breaks down rapidly in biologically active soil into carbon dioxide and water. It is also a Southern Cross Certified Allowed Input for organic and regenerative systems, although growers should confirm suitability with their own certifier before use.

A great tool in any grower’s kit

As with any contact herbicide, results depend on coverage. If the spray doesn’t reach the green tissue, it doesn’t work. FireHawk doesn’t spread like a dye, but needs to be applied like paint, covering the areas you want to target.

Where FireHawk earns its place is as a different mode of action that can be included in a mixed approach to weed control.

“It can be used alone, in rotation, or as a tank-mix partner with glyphosate or glufosinate,” says Richard. “Rotating away from a single chemistry gives glyphosate a break and helps bring resistant populations back under control before they reach the point that Mornington Peninsula vineyard found itself in.”

It also suits both conventional blocks and those run under organic or regenerative programs, which matters for growers managing a mix of both, or considering a transition, especially given current consumer sentiment trend towards organic products.

Learnings from the Mornington Peninsula case

The Mornington Peninsula result wasn’t about finding a stronger version of the same thing. The grower had already tried that. It was about attacking the weed through a pathway its resistance couldn’t defend against, and making sure the product reached the target.

For growers watching resistant ryegrass or fleabane creep further along the vine row each season, that is an approach worth trying sooner rather than later.

For more information, visit: https://firehawkbioherbicide.com.au/

content:
Priscilla and Iris of Skillogalee Cellar Door. Image courtesy Clare Valley Wine & Grape Association

Skillogalee Estate has been named the inaugural winner of The Praestantia Award for Clare Valley Cellar Door Excellence, a new award recognising outstanding hospitality, service and visitor experience across the Clare Valley.

Presented by the Clare Valley Wine & Grape Association (CVWGA), The Praestantia Award celebrates cellar door teams that go above and beyond to create memorable, customer-focused experiences characterised by warmth, professionalism, authenticity and a strong sense of place. The name Praestantia (pronounced press-TAN-shee-uh) is derived from the Latin word for excellence and distinction.

Crabtree Wines and O’Leary Walker Wines received honourable mentions for the “high standard” of their cellar door experiences during the judging process.

CVWGA explained that the award is grounded in its newly launched Clare Valley Customer Service Excellence Staff Training Program and was created to establish a “regional benchmark” for cellar door hospitality and to “recognise the important role cellar door teams play in shaping visitors’ perceptions of the Clare Valley”.

CVWGA executive officer Cherry Stowman said the award was designed to recognise the enormous contribution cellar door teams make to the region’s reputation.

“A cellar door experience is about so much more than the wine in the glass. Our cellar door teams are often the people who introduce visitors to Clare Valley, share our stories and inspire them to explore more of the region, return in the future and recommend Clare Valley to others,” she said.

Venues were assessed anonymously through a mystery shopping program conducted by Wine Tourism Australia. Trained mystery shoppers visited each participating venue three times, with visits scheduled across the judging period “to provide a robust assessment of the customer experience”. Scores and qualitative feedback were independently reviewed before the overall winner was determined.

The assessment criteria included “the warmth of the welcome, accessible and inclusive service, how well staff discovered and responded to individual guest interests, the quality of the tasting experience, regional storytelling, professionalism, advocacy for the broader Clare Valley and the farewell and ongoing connection with visitors”.

“The mystery shopping process allowed us to assess the experience through the eyes of a genuine visitor, and Skillogalee Estate should be incredibly proud to be the inaugural recipient of this award. We also congratulate Crabtree Wines and O’Leary Walker Wines on receiving honourable mentions in what was a very strong field,” said Stowman.

Skillogalee Estate received a handcrafted glass trophy created by South Australian glass artist Llewellyn Ash. Designed as a perpetual award, the sculptural piece was “conceived to reflect excellence and distinction while capturing the warmth, hospitality, landscape and sense of connection that underpin the Clare Valley visitor experience”.

The Praestantia Award will now be presented annually, “establishing an ongoing benchmark for cellar door excellence and celebrating the people and venues helping create exceptional visitor experiences across the Clare Valley”.
